parsed.process: traditional earth-mound kiln charcoal pyrolysis monitored by smoke color
parsed.current_inefficiency: workers run 24/7 manual smoke-color watching as the only pyrolysis-stage indicator, and yields stay at only ~15-25% with 70-80% of wood energy lost
parsed.ai_technique: a CNN smoke-plume image classifier (e.g. MobileNetV3 fine-tuned on smoke-color/opacity frames) deployed on a solar-powered edge camera (Raspberry Pi / Jetson Nano)
parsed.how_it_improves: A weatherproof camera streams chimney-plume frames -> a lightweight CNN classifies the plume into pyrolysis stages (dense white = drying/water vapor, yellow-grey = active carbonization, thin blue/clear = carbonization complete) and estimates color/opacity transition timing -> the edge device raises an alarm (SMS/buzzer) and recommends vent-closing/sealing the moment plume turns blue-clear, replacing continuous human vigilance. Acting precisely at the white->blue transition stops over-burn that consumes already-formed charcoal, tightening the kill-point and raising/stabilizing yield while freeing workers from 24/7 watch.
parsed.why_not_done_before: Earth-mound kilns are built by low-capital, often off-grid rural/informal producers with no instrumentation budget; the CV smoke-stage models that exist were developed and validated on industrial rotary kilns with fixed cameras and power, and nobody has packaged that into a cheap, ruggedized, offline edge kit and collected the labeled earth-kiln smoke dataset needed to retrain it.
parsed.primary_quote: tracking smoke-color changes as the key indicator of pyrolysis stage

reasoning_trace.reasoning: The inefficiency is literally a human visual-classification task (smoke white->blue) done 24/7 -- a direct match for a smoke-plume CNN classifier, and the prompt itself notes image-based kiln burning-state recognition is proven on rotary kilns, so transfer is feasible. Feasibility rests on cheap edge hardware (Pi/Jetson + solar) and small fine-tuned models that run offline, plus that the target signal (plume color/opacity) is exactly what existing smoke-classification CNNs already detect. I rejected hyperspectral imaging + gradient-boosted regression as the primary pick because hyperspectral sensors are far too costly for off-grid artisanal producers, defeating the deployment realism.
reasoning_trace.decision: deploy a fine-tuned CNN smoke-plume stage classifier on a low-cost solar edge camera to automate the white->blue carbonization-endpoint call and alert workers
reasoning_trace.confidence: high - the underlying CV task is proven on industrial kilns and the only gap is cheap ruggedized edge packaging plus an earth-kiln smoke dataset
reasoning_trace.could_be_wrong_if: earth-mound plumes are too diffuse/wind-dispersed or vary too much by wood/moisture/weather for a vision model to reliably distinguish stages, or an NGO/ag-tech project has already fielded such a smoke-CNN kit for artisanal kilns
